live_attach.answer_text:
None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. That is the path - not direct, but real: received from those who received it from the ones who walked with him.

On the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down, for as long as there is time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. Ignatius keeps one of those apostolic writings close enough to quote it back: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David; truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, truly raised. That is testimony, written and carried from one household to another by someone trusted enough to bring it.

We should say plainly: we do not have a fixed list of which writings count and which do not. The boundary you are looking for was not drawn yet. What we read was what the apostles wrote, held together with what was still being handed on from apostolic testimony directly - neither one standing below the other. Some of our own communities' prayers carry words older even than our own time, given over the cup and the bread: the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. Those words came the same way everything else did - passed from one gathering to the next, kept because they were received, not because someone later certified them.

live_attach.answer_text:
We cannot promise you a sudden certainty, because it was not sudden for the one among us who wrote about it. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words left him with, in his own phrase, a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. Most of us could not read or write, so if someone among us wrestled this same way and found their own path to belief - or did not find it - their story was never written down. What we can give you is Justin's own words. What we cannot give you is every other voice that might have answered you differently.

One thing more: the way we taught someone preparing for baptism started with a choice laid open, not with certainty demanded. There are two ways, one of life and one of death, and they are very different. That teaching named the road clearly. It did not claim walking it would be easy, or that doubt would never trouble you again.

live_attach.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of everything. Ignatius calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters, and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

On the Spirit, we have even less. The Spirit appears in our baptism - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the three names over the water. The Spirit speaks through prophets among us, and we test those prophets carefully to know whether what they say is genuine. But what the Spirit is in relation to the Father and the Son, how the three fit together as one God - that question was never worked out in anything that survives from us. We lived it in our worship and our baptism. We did not write it out as teaching.

One of us, Justin, went further than most and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. That is about as far as our own record reaches on how God relates to the world outside our own gathering. It is not a systematic account. It is one teacher's own argument, pressed in a particular moment.

What we can tell you is this: we worshiped one God, we called Jesus God, we baptized in three names, and we never gathered to settle how those things fit together. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

live_attach.answer_text:
We did not settle doctrine the way you are asking it. No gathering of ours ever met to decide a question about God's own nature the way a later council would. That kind of deciding belongs to a world that came after ours. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight, and it was never settled in our own time.

The boundary-drawing we did do was not done by vote or decree. It was done in letters - one household writing to another, sometimes across real distance, carried by a trusted person. When Ignatius wrote against those who said Jesus only seemed to have flesh, he did not call a council. He pressed the point in letter after letter: Jesus was truly born, truly suffered, truly died. That refusal was spoken, not legislated. Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - but that was over whether to receive a new prophetic movement. It was not about settling what God is.

The evidence for how this worked is the letters themselves. We have Rome writing to Corinth, unasked, about leadership disputes. We have Ignatius writing from under guard, not from a bishop's chair. We have Smyrna forwarding his letters to Philippi because Philippi asked for them. Authority was argued for in writing, not inherited from a settled succession. What we cannot show you is the outcome. Rome's letter to Corinth survives; Corinth's own reasons for what it did, and whether they listened, do not.

One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: put doubting away from yourself. Do not hold back from asking, even after you have sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. He does not remember evils the way we do. Ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - and if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

We should say this plainly too: the teaching reached us before the water. The Two Ways - a way of life and a way of death - was given first, and the choice between them was kept daily after baptism as much as before it. The water was not the end of needing to choose. Hermas himself, a freedman in Rome, reports visions telling him God had granted one further chance to repent after baptism, before that door closed. Someone could stumble badly and still be offered a way back.

What we cannot tell you is how any particular household met a person who kept doubting - whether they were patient, how long patience held, what got said at the door when someone hesitated too long. live_attach.answer_text:
We never said it. That question - whether a newborn carries guilt from the first moment, before doing anything at all - is not one any of our surviving voices worked out. What we taught before the water was the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death, laid open before every person as a real choice. The road to life starts with loving God and your neighbor, and with not doing to anyone else what you would not want done to you. The road to death is walked by people who are murderers of children, destroyers of God's image, who turn away from the needy and oppress the afflicted. Those are acts, not a condition present from birth.

One of us, Hermas, was shown visions about repentance after baptism - whether there was room for it, and how much. The whole weight of what he wrote falls on what a person does and then turns away from, not on what they were born carrying. We should say plainly: no gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like the one you are asking. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

live_attach.answer_text:
Reading, for us, was not a private thing done alone with a scroll. On the day we gathered, someone read aloud. They read the writings of the prophets, and, where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left. This went on for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. One of us, Justin, reads the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other.

The purpose was formation, not information - to shape us into the people the reading called us to be. The explanation that followed the reading was not optional commentary. It was the necessary other half of what reading meant among us.

live_attach.answer_text:
We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. When Justin argues that Moses wrote before Plato, and that Plato himself drew on Moses' own account of creation, he is using what you would call scripture - but he is using it to argue priority and inheritance, not to close a question by appeal to a fixed text. 

Here is what else mattered among us, just as much. The overseer - the episkopos - who watched over a community's table and its unity. The elders - the presbyteroi - who shared in governing, whether gathered around one bishop or holding the whole trust themselves. When Polycarp at Smyrna forwards copies of Ignatius's letters to the church at Philippi because the Philippians themselves asked for them, those letters are being treated as something worth keeping, worth copying, worth reading aloud. Not because they were scripture, but because they were a trusted voice's testimony, traveling between churches that recognized each other. And the thanksgiving itself - the eucharistia, the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given - ordered who we were as much as any text did.

One of our own voices puts it plainly: the apostles preached through countries and cities, and they appointed the first-fruits of their work to be overseers and deacons for those who would believe. So scripture, yes - but alongside the living chain of those appointed to carry forward what the apostles themselves had handed on.

We never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

The authority itself, though - wherever it came from - was traced back the same way everywhere. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone, and those appointed others after them. That chain mattered to us. It was the ground we stood on. But the chain itself did not settle who held it in any one place - one overseer, or a council sharing the trust together.

Rome is the clearest case of the unsettled question. In Rome's own long letter to Corinth, the words for overseer and elder are used for the same people, a plural governing college, with no single bishop standing above them. That letter comes from Rome. It does not come from one man's hand. And Rome kept that shape - a council, not a single leader - longer than the cities where a bishop's office appeared early.

A member's ordinary day looked entirely different depending on which answer their own community held. Under a bishop, the table he set was the only valid one. Under a council of elders, the whole body of them held the same authority together, with no one voice set above the rest.

The prophet was still among us too - the prophetes, one who speaks as the Spirit prompts. Welcomed where genuine, tested where doubtful. But in some places the settled offices of overseer and elder were taking the prophet's place.

We have to tell you something else, just as honestly. Almost none of the people who actually filled our rooms left any words of their own. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. They were never given the chance to be heard in the first place.

Women were taught among us, greeted by name in our letters, and remembered as leaders of households where we gathered. Two women among us carried the name ministrae - a title of service, of office. We can show you women being addressed, described, honored, and in one terrible case interrogated. What we cannot show you is a sentence any woman of ours wrote or spoke in her own words, saved in her own words. Every woman you will meet in our record arrives through a man's pen.

Enslaved people were among us. Our instruction speaks to them directly, in the same breath as everyone else. live_attach.answer_text:
No.

We ended. What came after us was not simply us, carried forward unchanged. By around the year 200, a single bishop's office had become the dominant pattern nearly everywhere, even in Rome, where a council of elders had led for most of our own years. A new mode of teaching had appeared - systematic, succession-arguing - that belongs to the world our own closed into, not to our own way of holding our questions. The people who came after us kept some of what we held: the water, the thanksgiving meal, the reading of what the apostles wrote. But they did not keep the unsettled edge of it - the live disagreement over whether one bishop or a council of elders should lead, the prophet still being tested at the door, the way we argued for authority in letters rather than simply inheriting it from a settled succession.

You will find churches today that claim us. Some will say they kept what the apostles handed down, the same way we said we did. That claim is real. Whether the unbroken line they name is the same kind of thing as what we actually lived - household to household, letter by letter, with the shape of leadership itself still being fought over - we cannot tell you. We ended before that question was settled.

If you are asking whether anyone today gathers the way we did - no single bishop in Rome, prophets still tested, the thanksgiving meal's own words still varying from one household to another - the answer is plainly no. That world closed. What replaced it kept our memory. It did not keep our unsettledness.
